```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
```

**isoniche** estimates the habitat niche breadth of species from counts in
several habitats, corrected for abundance. Classic indices (Levins' B,
1 - Gini of habitat proportions, Shannon...) make rare species look like
specialists: when a species is rare, its few individuals sit in its
preferred habitat; when it is abundant, it spills into others. isoniche
uses *isodars*, the relationships between a species' densities in pairs of
habitats, to predict where individuals settle at any total abundance, and
reports two numbers per species:

* **density-independent (DI) niche breadth**: how widely the species uses
  habitats when it is rare, at the *spillover abundance* where it first
  occupies all the habitats it uses;
* **density-dependent (DD) niche breadth**: how widely it uses habitats when
  it is abundant.

Both are on a 0-1 scale (0: one habitat only; 1: equal use of all
habitats) and, unlike classic indices, they can be compared among species
that differ in abundance.

This vignette walks through a complete analysis. The other vignettes go
into more detail:

* `vignette("data-preparation")`: data formats, effort, choosing habitats,
  absent habitats, grouping sites;
* `vignette("diagnostics")`: when to trust an estimate and what to do when
  a species is flagged;
* `vignette("method")`: how the method works (Granot, Dubiner & Belmaker
  2026).

## What you need

Counts of each species in two or more habitats, in many *replicates*:
sites, or repeated surveys of the same site. Replicates should span a range
of abundances, because isodars are estimated from how abundance in one
habitat changes with abundance in another. As a rule of thumb, aim for at
least 10 replicates per species, most of them sampling every habitat.

```{r setup}
library(isoniche)
```

## 1. Your data

isoniche works on data in long format, one row per species x site x
habitat, with the number of individuals counted. A habitat not sampled at a
site simply has no row; a habitat sampled where the species was not found
should have a row with a count of 0.

The package includes counts of 325 reef fish species in three habitats
(barrier reef, fringing reef, outer slope) at 13 sites around Moorea,
French Polynesia:

```{r data}
head(moorea_fish)
```

If your data are a community matrix (samples x species, as used by
**vegan**) with a separate table describing each sample, convert them with
`community_to_long()`:

```{r community}
comm <- matrix(c(12, 0, 3,
                  8, 2, 0,
                  0, 5, 9),
               nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(NULL, c("sp_a", "sp_b", "sp_c")))
samples <- data.frame(site = c("north", "north", "south"),
                      habitat = c("reef", "lagoon", "reef"))
community_to_long(comm, samples, site = "site", habitat = "habitat")
```

Several samples from the same site and habitat are pooled, and their
effort (here the number of samples) is summed into an `effort` column. If
samples differ in effort, for example in transect area, give that column
to `community_to_long()` and pass it on as `effort =` to the functions
below; set `reference_effort` to a natural unit such as one standard
transect. See `vignette("data-preparation")`.

## 2. Check coverage

Before estimating anything, check how well each species was sampled:

```{r coverage}
cov <- check_coverage(moorea_fish, species = "species", site = "site",
                      habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
cov[cov$species == "Chaetodon ornatissimus", ]
table(cov$status)
```

For each species and habitat, `n_sites` is the number of sites where the
species was recorded, `n_occupied` the number where it was found in this
habitat, and `status` says how the habitat will be treated: `"used"`,
`"absent"` (never found in it although it was sampled at several sites
where the species occurred; it counts as 0 and lowers niche breadth) or
`"undersampled"` (no records, but too few sites to tell).

## 3. Estimate niche breadth

We analyse 12 species that were recorded at almost every site, in every
habitat. `niche_breadth()` fits the isodars of every species, computes DI
and DD niche breadth and the spillover abundance, and gives bootstrap
confidence intervals by resampling whole sites (`n_boot` replicates; we use
99 to keep this vignette fast, but use 999 or more for publication):

```{r nb}
species <- c("Balistapus undulatus", "Chaetodon ornatissimus",
             "Chaetodon ulietensis", "Ctenochaetus binotatus",
             "Dascyllus flavicaudus", "Forcipiger longirostris",
             "Halichoeres marginatus", "Heniochus chrysostomus",
             "Parupeneus multifasciatus", "Sargocentron microstoma",
             "Scarus schlegeli", "Zebrasoma scopas")
fish <- moorea_fish[moorea_fish$species %in% species, ]

nb <- niche_breadth(fish, species = "species", site = "site",
                    habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance",
                    n_boot = 99, seed = 1)
nb
```

The result is a table with one row per species. The main columns:

* `nb_di` (with `nb_di_lower`, `nb_di_upper`): DI niche breadth and its
  confidence interval;
* `spillover_abundance`: the total abundance (individuals per sampling
  unit, here per site) at which the species first occupies every habitat it
  uses; DI niche breadth is measured there;
* `nb_dd`: DD niche breadth, the limit at high abundance;
* `flags`: diagnostics raised for the species.

```{r nb-table}
res <- as.data.frame(nb[c("species", "nb_di", "nb_di_lower", "nb_di_upper",
                          "spillover_abundance", "nb_dd", "nb_dd_lower",
                          "nb_dd_upper")])
res[-1] <- round(res[-1], 2)
res[order(-res$nb_di), ]
```

A species with high DI niche breadth uses several habitats even when rare:
its isodar intercepts are small, so it has no strongly preferred habitat. A
species with high DD niche breadth spreads evenly among habitats when
abundant: its isodar slopes are close to 1, so its habitats fill at similar
rates. The two need not agree; a species can be a specialist when rare and
a generalist when abundant, or the reverse.

## 4. Check the diagnostics

Every species gets logical `flag_*` columns. `summary()` counts them and
explains what to do about each:

```{r summary}
summary(nb)
```

`reversal` and `abandoned` describe the species rather than a problem: the
ranking of habitats changes with abundance, or a habitat used when the
species is rare is left empty when it is abundant. The others are warnings.
Here most species are flagged `unstable_bootstrap`: with only 13 sites, the
confidence intervals are wide (see the table above), and several DD
intervals reach 0. This is a property of the data, not of the method: niche
breadth is estimated from the spread of densities across sites, and 13
sites constrain it only loosely. More replicates narrow the intervals.

To keep only species without warnings:

```{r clean}
s <- summary(nb)
clean <- nb[nb$species %in% s$clean, ]
nrow(clean)
```

See `vignette("diagnostics")` for each flag.

## 5. Niche breadth across abundances

DI and DD niche breadth are the two ends of a curve: niche breadth as a
function of total abundance, much like a rarefaction curve. `iai_curve()`
computes it, and `plot()` draws it (here for four species):

```{r curve, fig.height = 5}
curves <- iai_curve(nb, n_boot = 49, seed = 1)
plot(curves, species = c("Chaetodon ornatissimus", "Forcipiger longirostris",
                         "Scarus schlegeli", "Zebrasoma scopas"))
```

Each curve starts at the species' spillover abundance (filled point, DI
niche breadth) and approaches DD niche breadth (dash on the right); dotted
lines are the bootstrap band and crosses mark preference reversals.

## 6. Compare species

Because the estimates do not depend on how abundant a species happened to
be, they can be compared among species, or related to traits. Ranks by DI
and by DD niche breadth can differ:

```{r compare, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5}
plot(nb$nb_di, nb$nb_dd, pch = 19, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "DI niche breadth", ylab = "DD niche breadth")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
cor(nb$nb_di, nb$nb_dd, method = "spearman")
```

Where two species' curves cross, which one is the broader generalist
depends on the abundance at which they are compared. These crossings are
listed in a table:

```{r crossings}
head(attr(curves, "crossings"))
```

## 7. Reporting

When reporting results, state:

* the habitats included, and which were treated as absent for each species;
* the sampling unit of abundance (`reference_effort`; see
  `vignette("data-preparation")`): DI niche breadth and spillover abundance
  depend on it, DD niche breadth does not;
* the isodar method (`dim`, by default pairwise isodars with inverse-variance
  weights) and where DD niche breadth was evaluated (`dependent_at`, by
  default the asymptote);
* the number of bootstrap replicates and the diagnostic thresholds, and how
  flagged species were handled;
* the package version (`packageVersion("isoniche")`) and the paper
  (`citation("isoniche")`).

## References

Granot, I., Dubiner, S. & Belmaker, J. (2026). Why abundance-based indices of
niche breadth are biased, and what can be done to improve them. *Ecology
Letters* (in revision). Itai Granot and Shahar Dubiner contributed equally.
